questions.question: What is TypeScript?
questions.correctAnswer: A typed superset of JavaScript, developed by Microsoft, that compiles to plain JavaScript and catches errors at development time.
wrongAnswers: A new runtime developed by Google that executes typed code directly in the browser, replacing JavaScript engines and catching errors only when the code runs in production.
A subset of JavaScript that removes dynamic features to make code run faster in Node.js.
A linter developed by Facebook that checks JavaScript code style at runtime.

questions.question: What are the advantages of TypeScript?
questions.correctAnswer: Early error detection, better autocomplete and refactoring, self-documenting code and safer maintenance in large projects.
wrongAnswers: Faster runtime execution, because browsers read the type annotations and use them to optimize the generated machine code for every function in large projects.
Faster runtime execution, since types are used by the browser to optimize code.
Smaller bundle size, since TypeScript removes unused code automatically.

questions.question: What are the primitive types?
questions.correctAnswer: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, symbol and bigint.
wrongAnswers: string, number, boolean, object, array, function and tuple, which are all represented as primitive values at runtime.
string, int, float, double, char, boolean and void, mirroring the primitive types available in Java and C#.
string, number, boolean, any, unknown and never.

questions.question: What is the any type?
questions.correctAnswer: It disables type checking for that value. It should be avoided because it removes TypeScript's safety.
wrongAnswers: A safe type for unknown values that requires narrowing before use.
A type representing values that never occur.
A type that accepts only primitive values, not objects.

questions.question: What is the unknown type?
questions.correctAnswer: A safe type for unknown values: you must narrow it (type narrowing) before using it.
wrongAnswers: A type that disables all checking for the value, allowing any operation without narrowing; it is just a newer alias for any introduced in TypeScript 3.
A type automatically assigned to variables declared without an initial value, which cannot be reassigned after the first assignment is made.
A type that disables all type checking, identical to any.

questions.question: What is the difference between any and unknown?
questions.correctAnswer: any allows any operation without checking; unknown requires a type check before use.
wrongAnswers: unknown allows any operation without checking; any requires a type check before use.
any is only for objects and unknown is only for primitives.
There is no difference; unknown is an alias of any introduced in TS 3.

questions.question: What is the never type?
questions.correctAnswer: It represents values that never occur, such as functions that always throw or impossible branches in exhaustive checks.
wrongAnswers: It represents a function that returns nothing useful, like void.
It represents null and undefined combined.
It represents a variable that can never be reassigned, like const.

questions.question: What is the void type?
questions.correctAnswer: It indicates that a function doesn't return a useful value.
wrongAnswers: It indicates a value that can never occur, such as the result of an infinite loop or a function that always throws.
It indicates that a variable or property is always null and can never hold any other value.
It indicates that a function can return any type.

questions.question: How do you declare a typed array?
questions.correctAnswer: string[] or Array<string>.
wrongAnswers: array<string> or [string]... using lowercase generic syntax.
List<string> or string() as in C#.
array<string> or [string]...

questions.question: What are tuples?
questions.correctAnswer: Arrays with a fixed length and fixed types per position, such as [string, number].
wrongAnswers: Objects with exactly two properties named first and second, used to return pairs of values from functions without creating a class.
Arrays that can grow to any length but can only contain values of a single type, such as number[] or string[].
Immutable sets of unique values, like Set.

questions.question: What is an interface?
questions.correctAnswer: A declaration that describes the shape of an object (properties and methods), which can be extended and implemented by classes.
wrongAnswers: A runtime object that validates the data passed to functions and throws an error when a required property is missing or has the wrong type.
A class that contains default implementations of methods, which other classes inherit by extending it with the implements keyword.
A type that can only describe unions and primitives.

questions.question: What is a type alias?
questions.correctAnswer: A name for any type, created with type, including unions, intersections, tuples and primitives.
wrongAnswers: A name for object shapes only, created with type, which supports declaration merging just like interfaces do.
A runtime variable that stores a type so it can be inspected later through reflection APIs.
A shortcut that renames a JavaScript class at compile time.

questions.question: What is the difference between interface and type?
questions.correctAnswer: Interfaces support declaration merging and extends; type accepts unions, tuples and conditional types. For objects, both work well.
wrongAnswers: type supports declaration merging; interfaces accept unions and conditional types.
Interfaces exist at runtime while types are erased.
Interfaces can only be used with classes, never with plain objects.

questions.question: What is type inference?
questions.correctAnswer: The compiler's ability to deduce a type from the assigned value without an explicit annotation.
wrongAnswers: The process of converting types into runtime checks automatically.
A feature that guesses types at runtime using typeof.
The ability to import types from other files without import statements.

questions.question: What are union types?
questions.correctAnswer: Types that accept one of several, such as string | number.
wrongAnswers: Types that merge several types into one, requiring every property, written as A & B.
Types that convert a value to another type at runtime, like Number(x).
Types that combine several into one, requiring all properties, such as A & B.

questions.question: What are intersection types?
questions.correctAnswer: They combine several types into one with A & B, requiring all properties.
wrongAnswers: They accept a value of one of several types, written as A | B, without requiring all properties.
They keep only the properties that A and B have in common, removing the rest from the result.
They compare two types and return a boolean.

questions.question: What are literal types?
questions.correctAnswer: Types that represent exact values, such as "admin" or 42, used in unions like "GET" | "POST".
wrongAnswers: Types written as string literals that are evaluated at runtime, so "admin" becomes a check that the value equals the string.
Types created automatically for every object literal in the code, which cannot be combined in unions or intersections.
Types that only allow template literal strings.

questions.question: What are optional properties?
questions.correctAnswer: Declared with ?, as in name?: string; the value may be undefined.
wrongAnswers: Declared with !, as in name!: string, which means the value may be null at runtime.
Declared with the optional keyword before the property name.
Properties with a default value that is filled in automatically by the compiler.

questions.question: What is readonly?
questions.correctAnswer: A modifier that prevents reassignment of a property after initialization.
wrongAnswers: A modifier that makes a property private to the class.
A modifier that freezes the object at runtime with Object.freeze.
A modifier that makes a property optional.

questions.question: What is an enum?
questions.correctAnswer: A set of named constants. They can be numeric or string-based; many prefer unions of literals because they are lighter.
wrongAnswers: A type that enumerates all the keys of an object at runtime.
A loop construct for iterating over object properties.
A special array type that only accepts numbers in sequence.

questions.question: How do you type a function?
questions.correctAnswer: By annotating parameters and return: function sum(a: number, b: number): number.
wrongAnswers: With Java-like syntax: function sum(number a, number b) -> number, declaring the type before each parameter.
With a JSDoc comment above the function, since TypeScript cannot annotate parameters inline.
With function sum(number a, number b) -> number.

questions.question: How do you define optional and default parameters?
questions.correctAnswer: (a: number, b?: number) for optional and (a: number, b = 10) for a default value.
wrongAnswers: (a: number, b!: number) for optional and (a: number, b: 10) for a default value, where the literal type sets the default.
(a: number, optional b: number) for optional and (a: number, default b = 10) for a default value.
(a: number, ?b: number) for optional and (a: number, b := 10) for a default value.

questions.question: What is a type assertion?
questions.correctAnswer: Telling the compiler a value's type with as, as in value as string. It does not convert at runtime.
wrongAnswers: Converting a value to another type at runtime with as, so value as string behaves like String(value) and changes the actual data.
A runtime check that throws if the value does not match the type.
A test assertion that verifies types in unit tests.

questions.question: What is the ! operator (non-null assertion)?
questions.correctAnswer: It asserts that a value is not null/undefined (obj!.x). Use with caution.
wrongAnswers: It negates a type, so !string means every type except string; useful for excluding cases.
It checks at runtime that the value is not null and throws a descriptive error otherwise.
It marks a property as required in an interface.

questions.question: What is optional chaining ?.?
questions.correctAnswer: It accesses properties safely, returning undefined if an intermediate value is nullish.
wrongAnswers: It throws a descriptive TypeError if any intermediate value in the chain is null or undefined.
It makes a property optional in a type declaration.
It returns the right-hand side if the left is null or undefined.

questions.question: What is nullish coalescing ???
questions.correctAnswer: It returns the right-hand side only if the left is null or undefined (unlike ||, which considers falsy values).
wrongAnswers: It returns the right-hand side whenever the left is any falsy value, including 0 and empty strings, exactly like the || operator.
It accesses nested properties safely, returning undefined when an intermediate value is missing instead of throwing an error.
It checks whether both sides are null and returns a boolean.

questions.question: What is tsconfig.json?
questions.correctAnswer: The compiler configuration file: options like target, module, strict, paths and included files.
wrongAnswers: The file that lists the npm dependencies and scripts of a TypeScript project, replacing package.json in projects that use tsc.
A file generated by tsc containing the compiled output's source maps.
The file where runtime environment variables are declared for TypeScript.

questions.question: What does the strict option do?
questions.correctAnswer: It enables a set of strict checks (strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, etc.), recommended for new projects.
wrongAnswers: It only enables JavaScript's "use strict" directive in the emitted files, without changing any type checking behavior in the compiler.
It makes the compiler stop at the first error it finds instead of reporting all of them, which speeds up feedback in large projects.
It forbids the use of classes and enums.

questions.question: What is noImplicitAny?
questions.correctAnswer: It raises an error when TypeScript implicitly infers any due to a missing annotation.
wrongAnswers: It forbids any explicit use of the any type anywhere in the code, including type assertions.
It converts every implicit any into unknown automatically.
It disables type inference so every variable must be annotated.

questions.question: What is strictNullChecks?
questions.correctAnswer: It makes null and undefined distinct types, preventing errors from accessing null values.
wrongAnswers: It removes null from the language entirely, so only undefined can be used to represent missing values.
It inserts runtime checks for null values in the emitted JavaScript and throws errors when they are accessed.
It forces every property to be initialized with null.

questions.question: How do you type classes?
questions.correctAnswer: By declaring properties with types and access modifiers (public, private, protected) and implementing interfaces with implements.
wrongAnswers: By placing a mandatory @Type() decorator above each property, since class fields cannot be annotated directly in TypeScript.
By declaring types only as constructor parameters, because properties declared in the class body cannot receive types or modifiers.
By using a @Type decorator above each property, which is required.

questions.question: What is a .d.ts file?
questions.correctAnswer: A type declaration file, without implementation, that describes JavaScript libraries.
wrongAnswers: A compiled JavaScript file with types embedded as metadata, used by Node to check values at runtime.
A debug file generated by tsc to trace type errors.
A data file containing test fixtures for typed tests.

questions.question: What is @types?
questions.correctAnswer: npm packages (such as @types/node) that provide type declarations for libraries written in JavaScript.
wrongAnswers: A built-in TypeScript namespace that contains the primitive types and must be imported in every file.
A folder in the project root where all interfaces and type aliases must be stored to be found by the compiler.
A decorator used to declare types on class properties.

questions.question: How is TypeScript executed?
questions.correctAnswer: It is transpiled to JavaScript by tsc (or esbuild/SWC/Babel) and the resulting JS runs in Node or the browser. Tools like tsx and ts-node run it directly.
wrongAnswers: Modern browsers and Node.js execute .ts files natively, reading the type annotations to validate values while the program runs, so no transpilation step is needed.
It is compiled to WebAssembly by tsc, and the resulting .wasm module runs faster than JavaScript in both Node.js and the browser.
Browsers execute .ts files natively, so no compilation is needed.

questions.question: What are generics?
questions.correctAnswer: They allow creating reusable components, functions and types that work with various types, such as function id<T>(x: T): T.
wrongAnswers: Types that accept any value without checking, similar to any, used when you don't know the type of a parameter, such as function id(x: any): any.
Built-in utility types such as Partial and Pick only.
Classes that can be instantiated without a constructor.

questions.question: How do you constrain a generic?
questions.correctAnswer: With extends: <T extends { id: number }>, requiring T to have a certain shape.
wrongAnswers: With implements: <T implements { id: number }>, requiring T to provide that shape.
With a where clause after the signature: <T> where T: { id: number }, as in C#.
With implements: <T implements { id: number }>.

questions.question: What is keyof?
questions.correctAnswer: It produces a union of a type's keys: keyof {a: 1; b: 2} results in "a" | "b".
wrongAnswers: It returns an array of the object's keys at runtime, like Object.keys.
It produces a union of a type's values: 1 | 2.
It checks whether a key exists in an object and returns a boolean.

questions.question: What is typeof in a type context?
questions.correctAnswer: It obtains the type of an existing variable or value: type T = typeof obj.
wrongAnswers: It returns a string literal type such as "object" or "string", matching JavaScript's typeof operator.
It creates a new variable with the same value as obj.
It checks at runtime whether a value matches a declared type.

questions.question: What are mapped types?
questions.correctAnswer: Types that transform each property of another type: { [K in keyof T]: ... }.
wrongAnswers: Types created from the Map data structure at runtime.
Types that map a function's parameters to its return type.
Types generated by source maps for debugging.

questions.question: What are conditional types?
questions.correctAnswer: Types that choose a result based on a condition: T extends string ? "yes" : "no".
wrongAnswers: Types that are only checked by the compiler when a corresponding runtime if statement evaluates to true.
Types that become optional depending on a compiler flag.
Types created with if/else blocks inside interfaces.

questions.question: What is the infer keyword?
questions.correctAnswer: Inside conditional types, it captures a type for reuse, as in T extends Promise<infer U> ? U : T.
wrongAnswers: It tells the compiler to infer the type of a variable at runtime.
It forces type inference on function parameters without annotations.
It converts any into the most specific type available.

questions.question: What is Partial<T>?
questions.correctAnswer: A utility that makes all of T's properties optional.
wrongAnswers: A utility that makes all of T's properties required, removing the ? modifier.
A utility that makes every property of T readonly and optional at once.
A utility that picks half of T's properties.

questions.question: What is Required<T>?
questions.correctAnswer: It makes all properties required.
wrongAnswers: It makes all properties of T optional, adding ? to each one.
It requires T to be an object type and fails compilation otherwise.
It removes null and undefined from T.

questions.question: What is Pick<T, K>?
questions.correctAnswer: It creates a type with only the K properties of T.
wrongAnswers: It creates a type with all properties of T except those listed in K.
It creates an object type whose keys are K and values are T.
It creates a type with all properties of T except K.

questions.question: What is Omit<T, K>?
questions.correctAnswer: It creates a type with all properties of T except K.
wrongAnswers: It creates a type with only the K properties of T, discarding the rest.
It removes from union T the members that are assignable to K.
It removes null and undefined from T.

questions.question: What is Record<K, V>?
questions.correctAnswer: It creates an object type with keys K and values V.
wrongAnswers: It creates a tuple type [K, V] used to represent key-value pairs.
It creates an interface whose property names are the members of V and whose values are the members of K.
It creates a Map instance with keys K and values V at runtime.

questions.question: What is Readonly<T>?
questions.correctAnswer: It makes all of T's properties read-only.
wrongAnswers: It freezes the object at runtime with Object.freeze, recursively.
It makes all properties of T private to the declaring class.
It makes only the top-level array of T immutable.

questions.question: What is ReturnType<T>?
questions.correctAnswer: It extracts a function's return type.
wrongAnswers: It extracts the types of a function's arguments and returns them as a readonly tuple, in declaration order.
It extracts the resolved value type of a Promise.
It extracts a function's parameter types as a tuple.

questions.question: What is Parameters<T>?
questions.correctAnswer: It extracts a function's parameter types as a tuple.
wrongAnswers: It extracts a function's return type as a single type.
It returns an object type keyed by the parameter names.
It returns an object with the parameter names as keys.

questions.question: What is Awaited<T>?
questions.correctAnswer: It gets the resolved type of a Promise, unwrapping recursively.
wrongAnswers: It wraps T in a Promise, producing Promise<T> for async return types.
It makes a function async at the type level, changing its return type automatically.
It waits for type checking to finish before compiling.

questions.question: What is NonNullable<T>?
questions.correctAnswer: It removes null and undefined from T.
wrongAnswers: It adds null and undefined to T, making it nullable.
It makes every property of T required and non-optional.
It throws a compile error if T can be null.

questions.question: What are Exclude and Extract?
questions.correctAnswer: Exclude<T, U> removes from T the members assignable to U; Extract<T, U> keeps only those members.
wrongAnswers: Exclude<T, U> keeps only the members of T that are assignable to U; Extract<T, U> removes those members from T.
Exclude removes properties from an object type; Extract picks properties from an object type, like Omit and Pick.
They are runtime functions that filter arrays by type.

questions.question: What is type narrowing?
questions.correctAnswer: Refining a broader type into a more specific one using typeof, instanceof, in, equality or guards.
wrongAnswers: Converting a specific type into a broader one, such as from a string literal to string or any, to make assignments more flexible.
Casting a value with as to a smaller type, which the compiler trusts without verifying, to reduce the number of possible types.
Reducing the number of types in a file to speed up compilation.

questions.question: What are type guards?
questions.correctAnswer: Expressions or functions that guarantee the type within a block, such as typeof x === "string".
wrongAnswers: Compiler flags that prevent the use of any.
Decorators that validate class property types at runtime.
Access modifiers that protect class members.

questions.question: What are type predicates?
questions.correctAnswer: Functions with an x is Type return that tell the compiler the argument is of that type.
wrongAnswers: Functions that return a boolean type literal only.
Generic constraints written with extends.
Assertions written with as const.

questions.question: What are discriminated unions?
questions.correctAnswer: Unions of objects with a common literal property (e.g., kind) that enables safe narrowing with switch.
wrongAnswers: Unions where each member must have completely different property names.
Unions that exclude members based on a compiler flag.
Unions of primitive types only, like string | number.

questions.question: How do you do an exhaustive check?
questions.correctAnswer: In the switch default, assign the value to never; if a case is missing, the compiler reports an error.
wrongAnswers: Add a default case that returns any, so the compiler considers every possible value handled and the switch complete.
Enable the exhaustive flag in tsconfig.json, which makes every switch statement report missing union cases automatically.
Add a default case that returns any, so all cases are covered.

questions.question: What is as const?
questions.correctAnswer: It makes a literal be inferred as immutable with the most specific types possible (readonly, literals).
wrongAnswers: It converts a let declaration into a const at runtime, preventing reassignment of the variable.
It freezes the object at runtime with Object.freeze, making nested properties immutable too.
It casts any value to a constant number type.

questions.question: What is the difference between interface extends and intersection &?
questions.correctAnswer: extends detects property conflicts with an error and is more performant; & combines types and may produce never on conflicts.
wrongAnswers: & detects property conflicts with a clear error and is faster to check, while extends silently produces never when properties conflict.
extends only works with classes and & only works with interfaces, so they are used in completely different situations.
There is no difference; they compile to identical declarations.

questions.question: What is declaration merging?
questions.correctAnswer: Interfaces with the same name in the same scope are merged into one, useful for extending library types.
wrongAnswers: Merging multiple .ts files into a single output file during compilation to reduce the number of modules.
Combining two type aliases with the same name into a union.
Merging a class and an enum into a single object at runtime.

questions.question: What are index signatures?
questions.correctAnswer: They define the type of dynamic keys: { [key: string]: number }.
wrongAnswers: They declare that every array index must be a positive integer, preventing negative or fractional indexes.
They create a runtime index for faster property lookups in large objects.
They define the index type of an array, which must always be number.

questions.question: What are template literal types?
questions.correctAnswer: String types built by interpolation, such as on${Capitalize<string>} (with backticks inside the type).
wrongAnswers: Types for HTML templates, used by frameworks like Angular to check bindings inside component templates.
Runtime template strings that validate their interpolated contents against a declared type and throw on mismatch.
Types that can only be used inside JSX.

questions.question: What are function overloads?
questions.correctAnswer: Multiple signatures for the same function, describing different combinations of parameters and return types.
wrongAnswers: Multiple implementations of the same function, each with its own body, selected at runtime by the argument types.
Methods redefined in subclasses using the override keyword, replacing the parent's implementation.
Functions that receive more arguments than declared.

questions.question: What is the abstract modifier?
questions.correctAnswer: It marks classes or methods that must be implemented by subclasses; abstract classes cannot be instantiated.
wrongAnswers: It marks classes that can be instantiated only once, implementing the singleton pattern at the type level.
It hides a method from the compiled JavaScript output while keeping it available for type checking.
It marks methods that run asynchronously.

questions.question: What is the difference between private and #private?
questions.correctAnswer: private only exists at compile time; #field is real JavaScript privacy at runtime.
wrongAnswers: #field only exists at compile time and is erased, while private is enforced by the JavaScript engine at runtime.
private is used for methods and #private for properties only; they cannot be used interchangeably.
There is no difference; # is just a shorter syntax.

questions.question: How do you type a React component with props?
questions.correctAnswer: By defining a props interface/type and applying it to the parameter: function Button({ label }: ButtonProps).
wrongAnswers: By passing the props type as a second function argument, as in function Button(props, ButtonProps), which React reads at runtime.
By annotating the component's return type as ButtonProps, so the compiler infers the expected props from the returned JSX.
By using PropTypes only, since TypeScript cannot type React props.

questions.question: How do you type useState in React?
questions.correctAnswer: With generics: useState<User | null>(null).
wrongAnswers: With a cast on the setter function: setUser as (u: User) => void.
It cannot be typed; useState always returns any in TypeScript.
It cannot be typed; useState always returns any.

questions.question: How do you type events in React?
questions.correctAnswer: With types like React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> and React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>.
wrongAnswers: With the native DOM Event type only, because React does not ship its own event type definitions for handlers.
With any, which is the type the React team recommends for event handlers to avoid compatibility issues between browsers.
With React.Event<"click"> and React.Event<"change">.

questions.question: How do you safely type an API response?
questions.correctAnswer: Define types and validate at runtime with libraries like Zod, since types disappear after compilation.
wrongAnswers: Annotate the fetch result with as MyType, which makes the compiler insert a runtime validation of the response body.
Use a .d.ts file for the API, which TypeScript checks against live responses.
Enable strict mode, which validates JSON responses automatically.

questions.question: How do you create a DeepPartial type?
questions.correctAnswer: type DeepPartial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] extends object ? DeepPartial<T[K]> : T[K] }.
wrongAnswers: type DeepPartial<T> = Partial<Partial<T>>, since applying Partial twice makes nested properties optional as well.
type DeepPartial<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: DeepPartial<T[K]> }.
type DeepPartial<T> = T extends object ? Partial<T> : never.

questions.question: What are covariance and contravariance?
questions.correctAnswer: Covariance allows using subtypes where a supertype is expected (return types); contravariance reverses it (parameters, under strictFunctionTypes).
wrongAnswers: Covariance applies to parameters and contravariance applies to return types.
They describe how types change between TypeScript versions.
Covariance means two types are identical; contravariance means they are incompatible.

questions.question: What is strictFunctionTypes?
questions.correctAnswer: It performs contravariant checking of function parameters, preventing unsafe assignments.
wrongAnswers: It requires every function and method to declare an explicit return type, failing compilation otherwise.
It makes function parameters bivariant for flexibility, allowing more assignments between callbacks.
It forbids arrow functions in favor of function declarations.

questions.question: What are variadic tuple types?
questions.correctAnswer: Tuples with spreads of generic types ([...T, ...U]), allowing you to type argument concatenation.
wrongAnswers: Tuples that can have any length and any element types, equivalent to any[] but with better autocomplete.
Functions that accept a variable number of type parameters, such as fn<A, B, C, ...>().
Arrays whose length is determined at runtime.

questions.question: What is key remapping in mapped types?
questions.correctAnswer: Using as to rename keys: { [K in keyof T as "get" + Capitalize<K & string>]: () => T[K] }.
wrongAnswers: Using the rename() utility type to change an object's keys at runtime while preserving their value types.
Using Record<V, K> to swap the keys and values of a type, so values become the new keys of the resulting type.
Using keyof to sort the keys of a type alphabetically.

questions.question: What are distributive conditional types?
questions.correctAnswer: Conditional types with a "naked" type parameter distribute over unions: T extends U ? X : Y is applied to each member.
wrongAnswers: Conditional types that apply only to the first member of a union, ignoring the remaining members unless wrapped in an array.
Conditional types that are distributed across multiple files for faster compilation.
Conditional types that convert unions into intersections automatically.

questions.question: How do you prevent distribution in conditional types?
questions.correctAnswer: By wrapping in tuples: [T] extends [U] ? ... : ....
wrongAnswers: By adding the nodistribute keyword before extends, as in T nodistribute extends U ? X : Y.
By disabling strict mode in tsconfig.json, which turns off distribution of conditional types globally.
By using T & {} extends U.

questions.question: What are branded types (opaque types)?
questions.correctAnswer: A technique of adding a phantom brand (string & { __brand: "UserId" }) to differentiate structurally identical types.
wrongAnswers: Types published by a vendor library and sealed so that consumers cannot extend or augment them with new properties.
Types encrypted by the compiler so their internal structure is hidden from consumers of a published package.
Types encrypted at compile time to hide their structure.

questions.question: How do you type a function that preserves literals?
questions.correctAnswer: Using generics with const (<const T>) or constraints like T extends string.
wrongAnswers: By annotating the parameter as any, which keeps literal types intact because any never widens values.
By using readonly on the return type only, which prevents the compiler from widening literal arguments.
By annotating the parameter as any so literals are kept.

questions.question: What is unique symbol?
questions.correctAnswer: A type for unique symbols, useful for keys and brands that never collide.
wrongAnswers: A runtime function that generates unique IDs for objects.
A type that forbids duplicate values in an array.
A modifier that makes a class a singleton.

questions.question: What is typed this?
questions.correctAnswer: You can declare the type of this as a fake first parameter: function f(this: Context); there is also the polymorphic this type.
wrongAnswers: You type this with a decorator such as @this(Context) placed above the function declaration.
this is always typed as any and cannot be annotated.
this can only be typed inside arrow functions.

questions.question: What are decorators?
questions.correctAnswer: Functions annotated with @ that modify classes and members. TS 5 supports ECMAScript standard decorators; experimentalDecorators keeps the old format.
wrongAnswers: Special comments starting with @ that only affect documentation generation tools and are ignored by the compiler and the runtime.
Functions that run only during compilation and are completely removed from the output, so they never have any effect at runtime.
Type annotations that add CSS styles to classes.

questions.question: What is module augmentation?
questions.correctAnswer: Extending types of existing modules with declare module "x" { ... }, e.g., adding fields to Express's Request.
wrongAnswers: Installing missing npm modules automatically when the compiler cannot find type declarations for an import.
Merging two separate modules into a single file at build time to reduce imports and improve tree shaking.
Increasing the size limit of a module's bundle.

questions.question: What is declare global?
questions.correctAnswer: It lets you add or change types in the global scope from within a module.
wrongAnswers: It declares a runtime global variable accessible from any file.
It makes all types in a file exported automatically.
It disables module scope for the entire project.

questions.question: What is isolatedModules?
questions.correctAnswer: It requires each file to be transpilable in isolation, needed for esbuild/SWC/Babel; it restricts re-exports of types without type.
wrongAnswers: It runs each module's type checking in a separate thread during compilation to speed up large builds.
It prevents modules from importing each other, forcing every file to be self-contained with no dependencies.
It bundles each module into its own output file.

questions.question: What is the difference between tsc and esbuild/swc?
questions.correctAnswer: tsc type-checks and emits JS; esbuild/SWC only strip types and transpile, much faster, without checking.
wrongAnswers: esbuild/SWC type-check more strictly than tsc, but are slower.
tsc only strips types; esbuild/SWC perform full type checking.
They are identical; esbuild and SWC are just tsc wrappers.

questions.question: What are project references?
questions.correctAnswer: A monorepo feature that splits the project into subprojects with incremental builds and typed dependencies (composite).
wrongAnswers: Links to external documentation pages declared in tsconfig.json so the editor can show them on hover.
Triple-slash /// <reference> comments that every file must include to import types from other files.
A list of npm packages that the project depends on.

questions.question: How does module resolution (moduleResolution) work?
questions.correctAnswer: It defines how imports are located: node10, node16/nodenext (respecting ESM/CJS and exports) and bundler.
wrongAnswers: It resolves version conflicts between npm packages by choosing the newest compatible version of each dependency.
It defines the order in which modules are executed at runtime.
It determines which modules are tree-shaken from the bundle.

questions.question: How do you correctly type Object.keys?
questions.correctAnswer: It returns string[] for structural safety; you cast as (keyof T)[] when you know the exact shape.
wrongAnswers: It returns any[], so you should always annotate the result as unknown[] and narrow each key manually.
It already returns (keyof T)[], so no cast is ever needed.
It returns a union of the object's values.

questions.question: What are recursive types?
questions.correctAnswer: Types that reference themselves, such as type Json = string | number | boolean | null | Json[] | { [k: string]: Json }.
wrongAnswers: Types that TypeScript forbids because self-references would cause the compiler to enter an infinite loop.
Types generated by recursive functions at runtime.
Types that repeat the same property multiple times.

questions.question: How do you infer types from a Zod schema?
questions.correctAnswer: With z.infer<typeof schema>, keeping validation and type in a single source.
wrongAnswers: With ReturnType<typeof schema>, which extracts the validated output type from the schema object.
With ReturnType<schema>, which extracts the validated type.
With schema.type, a property that holds the TypeScript type at runtime.

questions.question: What is the Function type and why avoid it?
questions.correctAnswer: It accepts any function without specifying parameters or return. Prefer specific signatures like (x: number) => void.
wrongAnswers: It only accepts arrow functions, so passing a function declaration or method to a Function parameter causes a compile error.
It is deprecated and always throws a compile error in strict mode, so code using it no longer builds.
It forces all functions to return void.

questions.question: How does infer work with tuples and functions?
questions.correctAnswer: It lets you extract parts, for example T extends (...args: infer A) => infer R ? [A, R] : never.
wrongAnswers: infer only works with Promise types; to extract parameters or return types you must use runtime reflection instead.
It infers function types at runtime by inspecting the arguments passed on the first call and caching the result.
It only works with Promises and cannot extract function parts.

questions.question: How do you type HOCs or composition functions generically?
questions.correctAnswer: With generics that preserve the original props and remove/inject props via Omit and intersections.
wrongAnswers: By typing every prop as any, because higher-order components cannot be typed generically in TypeScript.
By typing all props as any, since HOCs cannot be typed.
By duplicating the props interface for every wrapped component.

questions.question: What is "type widening"?
questions.correctAnswer: Widening literal types to their base type (let x = "a" becomes string), while const x = "a" keeps the literal.
wrongAnswers: Narrowing a base type to a literal type, so let x = "a" is inferred as "a" while const x = "a" becomes string.
Automatically converting every number type in the project into bigint when values exceed the safe integer range.
Increasing the strictness level of the compiler.

questions.question: How do you deal with libraries without types?
questions.correctAnswer: Install @types/..., create a .d.ts with declare module "lib", or use an isolated any as a last resort.
wrongAnswers: Disable TypeScript checking for the whole project with // @ts-nocheck in every file that imports the library.
Rewrite the library in TypeScript before using it.
Import it with require, which TypeScript types automatically.

questions.question: How do you reduce compile time in large projects?
questions.correctAnswer: Use incremental, project references, skipLibCheck, avoid overly complex types and run type checking in CI separately from the build.
wrongAnswers: Disable strict mode and replace complex types with any everywhere, which removes most of the work tsc has to do.
Merge all source files into a single huge file so tsc only needs to read and parse one file per build.
Put all code in a single file so tsc reads only once.

questions.question: What are abstract construct signatures?
questions.correctAnswer: abstract new () => T signatures that describe constructors of abstract classes.
wrongAnswers: Signatures that allow creating instances of abstract classes directly with new, bypassing the abstract restriction.
Constructor signatures that run only at compile time to validate class hierarchies.
Signatures that forbid a class from being extended.

questions.question: What is the using declaration (TS 5.2)?
questions.correctAnswer: A declaration of disposable resources that automatically calls [Symbol.dispose] when leaving scope.
wrongAnswers: A keyword for importing namespaces into the current file, similar to the using directive in C#.
A declaration that marks a variable as used so the compiler and linter stop warning about unused values.
A statement that loads a module synchronously.

questions.question: How do you type an event emitter safely?
questions.correctAnswer: With an event map (interface Events { login: User }) and generics on<K extends keyof Events>(event: K, cb: (payload: Events[K]) => void).
wrongAnswers: By typing every event name as string and every payload as any, then documenting the expected shapes in comments.
By creating a separate emitter class for every event and using the Function type for all registered callbacks.
By typing all events as string and all payloads as any.

questions.question: When do you use unknown in catch?
questions.correctAnswer: With useUnknownInCatchVariables (part of strict), the error is unknown, forcing you to check with instanceof Error before using it.
wrongAnswers: Only when the try block contains await, because synchronous errors are always typed as Error by the compiler.
Never; catch variables are always typed as Error.
Only when the try block contains async code.
